On the night Ramchandra Ray escaped, Udayaditya forced the door, drew his sword on Sitaram, disarmed him, and bound him so he himself could leave. On the night Udayaditya escaped prison, Sitaram threw the door open, almost carried him out, and led him away, while Udayaditya, helpless after long confinement, could only ask where to go and follow.

I'll read the three referenced files and answer from their content only.

Pratapaditya first ordered two Pathans to kill Basanta Ray at the Simultali inn on the way to Jessore; they instead lured away his retainers, and one could not bring himself to do the deed. Later Muktiyar Khan, with Pratapaditya’s signed death sentence, had soldiers infiltrate Raigarh in disguise; after evening prayers, Abdul killed the old king with a sword.
In Jessore’s inner quarters, disguised as a middle-aged woman; and in the king’s chamber at Chandradwip, as the court jester.
Mangala (Rukmini) poisons Surma with a drug prepared as medicine, and she dies.
Ramchandra Ray takes another wife, so when Vibha later arrives she finds she has no place in her own palace and her hopes of happiness vanish.

Rukmini coaxes Udayaditya into giving her the ring from his finger; it bears his engraved seal. Sitaram and Bhagavat then write a forged petition, as if the Yubaraj were accusing Pratapaditya of treason before the Emperor, and stamp it with that seal. Bhagavat delivers the petition to Pratapaditya, claiming a servant of Udayaditya was taking it to Delhi, and Pratapaditya orders Udayaditya imprisoned on the strength of it.

Udayaditya overpowered Sitaram to let Ramchandra escape, after which Sitaram and Bhagavat were dismissed. When Udayaditya then paid them stipends, Pratapaditya forbade any further aid. Surma secretly continued the payments through a maid, and when Pratapaditya learned of it he ordered her sent to her paternal home.

The song expresses Basanta Ray’s sense of being left alone after those he loved have gone: what remains is emptiness, they no longer answer, and he has no spirit left to live by himself. He first hums it alone on the Raigarh veranda at sunset, a private melancholy for absent loved ones; later, in Jessore, he sings it slowly while holding Vibha’s hand after finding the inner quarters silent and empty.

Rukmini failed to halt the midnight flight, so Udayaditya and Basanta Ray reached Raigarh. She then told Pratapaditya they had escaped together; he sent Muktiyar Khan with a death sentence for the King of Raigarh. Remaining there, she led the soldiers to Udayaditya. Once he was seized, Muktiyar entered the fort and had Basanta Ray beheaded.

Pratapaditya received Ramchandra with delayed, sparse ceremony and cold indifference, barely greeting him before turning to other business and dismissing him as “my boy.” Later, Ramchandra’s court daily mocks Pratapaditya as a two-generation upstart of low origin, treats any comparison as insolence, and holds that marrying into Ramchandra’s house already redeems Jessore’s line—while Ramchandra, pleased, uses that scorn as honor and revenge.

Rukmini left Raigarh, took the name Mangala, and settled on Jessore’s outskirts. Befriending the palace servants, she sought to rule Udayaditya’s heart and the kingdom. When the queen sent for her tantric medicine to win him from Surma, Mangala spent five days preparing poison; Surma died of it. Later, in a storm, Rukmini entered his dark chamber, claimed he had ruined her, and took his ring.

Udayaditya’s early wish not to have been born crown prince—feeling unfit to rule and already thinking of abandoning court—ends when, brought as a prisoner, he tells Pratapaditya he is not worthy of the kingdom and begs release from the throne. He swears before Ma-Kali never to claim even an iota of Jessore, sit on its throne, or touch its scepter, naming Samaraditya heir, then leaves for Kashi.

Nayanchand, fearing Pratapaditya’s wrath, delivers Ramchandra’s letter of renunciation to the Mahishi instead of the king. On Basanta Ray’s advice she conceals its true contents and announces that Ramchandra has written asking for Vibha to be sent to Chandradwip, so Vibha believes her husband has forgiven her and summoned her home.

Pratapaditya blocked the canal with large sal-wood logs, but Rammohan and his men hauled the boat up and over them while the guards’ stones fell short and they scrambled for a gun, powder, and bullets; the chase boat then came too late.

When forced to part from Udayaditya, Basanta Ray played his sitar furiously until tears stopped him, then left it behind, saying he would not play it anymore. Later, with Udayaditya imprisoned, the sitar was no longer with him; he said it was there, but its strings had broken and it could no longer be tuned.

Before, he involved himself in subjects’ affairs and would have stopped an official beating a subject without considering the consequences. After Surma’s death, fear of Pratapaditya made him hesitate; he called off going to stop a planned raid, fled indoors when a subject begged for mercy, and no longer dared even to send secret help.
He frees imprisoned Udayaditya during the prison fire and leads him to safety.

He carries Ramchandra on his back down a rope of knotted sheets from the palace roof, then grips the rope in his teeth and lowers him into the boat. Later he lifts the fainted Vibha, carries her out of the palace, and puts her in a palanquin.

In Jessore she is loaded with eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and an elaborate coiffure. In Chandradwip she refuses a palanquin, goes dressed as a common woman and beggar, enters like a maidservant, and the king takes her for a beggar seeking alms.

In his bedchamber after Surma’s death, the window is the empty place of her absence: he sits there amid unchanged moonlight, garden, and breeze, hoping she will reappear. In the prison cell, the small window becomes the only space of inner freedom—sky and birds promise that his cage will break—while the bed away from it is darkness and captivity.

Sitaram, penniless, borrowed from widow Rukmini under flirtatious pretenses—pet names, mock-romance, unpaid “loans”—while they secretly schemed. After Udayaditya’s imprisonment he cursed her, nearly struck her, and threatened to burn her house and ruin her face. She answered with hatred, claiming the Yubaraj as hers. Later, believing her dead, he went to steal her money and found her alive. She vowed to kill him and the Yubaraj and smear herself with their ashes; when he tried affection again she fetched a blade. He fled as she struck the floor where he had stood.

Sitaram first has the guardhouse set alight so the watch, including the men at Udayaditya’s door, abandon their posts; he then pulls the prince out under the pretext that the prison itself is burning and sends him away by boat. After the escape, his men keep the blaze alive by bungling the firefighting, torch the empty cell, and plant bones, a skull, and Udayaditya’s sword in the flames. Shouts that the prince was heard screaming and that the roof has collapsed follow, so the court takes the melted sword and the rumor of death as proof he perished, covering the flight until the truth leaks.
He is ungrateful, treating the rescue as inevitable and done only for Vibha’s sake, and joins his court in mocking Udayaditya as Pratapaditya’s son.

Pratapaditya dismisses the Emperor of Delhi as no real threat. Bhagavat later forges a petition, sealed in Udayaditya’s name, as if the prince were charging Pratapaditya with treason before that Emperor to seize the kingdom, then delivers it to Pratapaditya as a letter intercepted on its way to Delhi, turning the dismissed specter into the charge against his son.

While Surma lived in the palace she dressed Vibha’s hair to Vibha’s own liking, against the Mahishi’s taste. After Surma’s disappearance Vibha still sits at braiding time waiting for her; evening comes, the hair stays unbraided, and Surma never arrives. Later her unkempt hair marks that no one remains to tend her.
